title: The secret life of the octopus
text: The octopus is without doubt one of the ocean's most {{1}} (MYSTERY) creatures. Scientists describe its intelligence as genuinely {{2}} (REMARK), noting that octopuses can solve puzzles, open jars and even recognise individual keepers. Their eight arms contain more neurons than their brain, giving each arm a degree of {{3}} (INDEPENDENT). Perhaps strangest of all is their talent for disguise: an octopus can change both colour and skin {{4}} (TEXTURE) in less than a second. Some researchers argue that such {{5}} (FLEXIBLE) could only have evolved under intense pressure. Unfortunately, captive octopuses often show signs of {{6}} (BORE), escaping tanks and dismantling equipment. Their short lives — usually just two years — make their achievements all the more {{7}} (ASTONISH). Protecting their deep-sea habitats is now seen as a scientific {{8}} (NECESSARY) rather than a luxury.

gaps.explanation: 'skin texture' — the noun here keeps the base form.
'signs of boredom' — the state of being bored.
'a scientific necessity' — noun form of necessary.

title: How coffee conquered the world
text: Coffee's rise from Ethiopian legend to global habit is a story of trade and obsession. By the seventeenth century, coffee houses had become centres of {{1}} (POLITICS) debate; some rulers briefly banned them, fearing revolution. Coffee's stimulating effect comes from caffeine, a natural chemical the plant produces for its own {{2}} (PROTECT). Today, coffee is grown in over seventy countries and supports the {{3}} (LIVE) of some 125 million people. Yet the industry faces an uncertain future: rising temperatures are making traditional growing regions less {{4}} (SUIT). Scientists are developing more {{5}} (RESIST) varieties, though purists complain about the taste. Coffee drinkers remain fiercely {{6}} (LOYAL) to their favourite blends. For millions of people, the morning cup is simply {{7}} (DISPENSE) — a small daily ritual. Few products can match its combination of {{8}} (POPULAR) and profitability.

gaps.explanation: 'for its own protection' — noun from protect.
'fiercely loyal' — the adjective keeps the base form.
'its combination of popularity and profitability' — noun forms of both adjectives.

title: Ada Lovelace, the first programmer
text: Ada Lovelace, born in 1815, is now celebrated as a pioneer of computing, yet her {{1}} (CONTRIBUTE) was ignored for a century. Daughter of the poet Byron, she was educated in mathematics by her anxious mother, who hoped numbers would discourage any poetic {{2}} (INCLINE). When Ada met Charles Babbage, she was immediately fascinated by his design for a mechanical {{3}} (CALCULATE) engine. Her notes on the machine include what is now regarded as the first computer {{4}} (OPERATE) in history. More strikingly, she foresaw that such machines could manipulate any symbols, not just numbers — an idea of extraordinary {{5}} (DEEP). Babbage, ironically, showed less {{6}} (ENTHUSIASTIC) for this abstraction than she did. Ada died young, and her work sank into {{7}} (OBSCURE) until the twentieth century. Today, her notes are admired as a triumph of scientific {{8}} (IMAGINE).

gaps.explanation: 'calculating engine' — Babbage's machine was a calculating engine.
'computer operation' — the noun from operate; the notes describe operations.
'showed less enthusiasm' — the noun form here.

title: Living walls
text: Vertical gardens, or 'living walls', are transforming city architecture. A living wall is a whole surface covered in plants, watered by {{1}} (CONCEAL) irrigation systems. Their benefits go far beyond {{2}} (APPEAR). The plants insulate buildings, cutting energy use, and their leaves trap dust and pollution, measurably improving air {{3}} (QUALIFY). In hot summers a living wall can keep a facade twenty degrees cooler, an effect that has made them {{4}} (INCREASE) popular with city planners. Maintenance, however, is demanding: systems fail if pumps break, and {{5}} (REPAIR) can be costly. The world's largest living wall, in Milan, contains over 44,000 plants and has become a tourist {{6}} (ATTRACT). Critics dismiss such projects as temporary {{7}} (FASHION), but research increasingly supports their {{8}} (EFFECT) at cooling streets and cleaning air.

gaps.explanation: 'air quality' — the related noun is quality.
'repairs can be costly' — the plural noun.

title: The psychology of queues
text: Queues are a strange form of organised {{1}} (PATIENT). We join them daily, yet psychologists find them endlessly {{2}} (INTEREST). Research shows that waiting feels longer when it is {{3}} (EXPLAIN), unoccupied time is painful, and — crucially — fairness matters more than length. A queue that jumps ahead of us enrages us even when the total wait is unchanged. Airports have exploited this by moving baggage claim further from arrivals: passengers walk rather than wait, and complaints have dropped {{4}} (DRAMA). Supermarkets, meanwhile, prefer to hide the mathematics: several shorter queues feel fairer than one long queue, even when they are less {{5}} (EFFICIENT). Some companies now offer virtual queues, promising a text message instead of standing in line. The technology is {{6}} (DOUBT) clever, but it removes the chance to chat to strangers, which some sociologists regret. Queue behaviour also changes with culture: in some countries the gentle {{7}} (PRESS) of a crowd counts as a place in line, while in Britain a row of shopping baskets marks the social {{8}} (ORDER) of the queue itself.

gaps.explanation: Queues cause interest: they are interesting.

gaps.hint: negative participle: with no reason given
gaps.explanation: 'unexplained' waits feel longer — negative prefix un-.
'gentle pressure of a crowd' — noun from press.
'social order of the queue' — the noun keeps the base form.
